issues.body: `route_token = os.environ.get("ALERT_TOKEN") or registry_token` still treats `REGISTRY_ALERT_TOKEN` as the private destination credential. With `ALERT_REPO=private/alerts`, no `ALERT_TOKEN`, and a registry token that can read the destination, the live probe returns private and `_alert_route` returns `("private/alerts", registry_token)`. This crosses the documented two-token boundary and can silently lose the best-effort alert when the registry-scoped token cannot write to the private repository. The default-route self-test now codifies the defect: after leaving `ALERT_TOKEN` unset, it expects `(("private/alerts", "t0"), ...)` rather than registry fallback with no probe.
issues.fix_hint: Use only `ALERT_TOKEN` as the candidate private-route token. If it is absent, return `(registry_repo, registry_token)` without issuing a visibility probe. Add a distinct-token test with `ALERT_REPO` and `REGISTRY_ALERT_TOKEN` set but `ALERT_TOKEN` absent that asserts registry fallback and zero probe calls; make the uninjected live-probe test set an explicit `ALERT_TOKEN` and assert that token is used for both the probe and private return.
issues.title: Missing ALERT_TOKEN still selects the private route with the registry token

verdict.summary:
> 🤖 SPARQ agent

The round-3 credential-boundary defect remains. Although the new routing matrix adds visibility checks and correctly returns the registry token on rejected routes, `_alert_route` still defines the candidate private-route token as `ALERT_TOKEN or REGISTRY_ALERT_TOKEN`. Consequently, a deployment with `ALERT_REPO` set, `ALERT_TOKEN` absent, and a registry-scoped token present still probes and selects the private repository using the registry credential. The new default-route self-test explicitly expects that unsafe selection. This is materially the same major finding as round 3, so progress is stagnant.
